# @aponiajs/testing

> Boot an Aponia application for a test with one call, replace a provider for one boot, and tear it down without leaking a listener. It boots a real application through `AponiaFactory.create`; what it adds is sane defaults, provider overrides, and a stop a case can rely on.

**This is not a test runner and not a mocking framework.** Every `test`, `it`, and `expect` stays the runner's — this package depends on none of them and works beside `bun:test`, `vite-plus/test`, and `node:test` alike. `overrideProvider` replaces one provider's descriptor in the compiled module graph: it does not record calls, does not stub one method of a real object, and has no module-interception macro, so a dependency a module imported directly is beyond its reach. A case that needs a call log writes its own object and passes it with `useValue`.

**This is not an in-memory HTTP server.** `application.handle(new Request(...))` calls the real route table, the real container, and the real handlers with no socket bound; it fakes nothing. `listen()` is the opposite — it binds a real port, and exists only because a WebSocket upgrade needs one. A reader who wants none of this should keep using `@aponiajs/platform-elysia` directly.

**A token no module in the graph provides is refused at build time** with `AponiaError` and the code `MISSING_PROVIDER`, carrying `{ token }`. A stub registered for a token nothing provides would otherwise leave every test green while the code under test used the real dependency.

## What this package exports

```ts
import { createTestApplication, TestApplication } from "@aponiajs/testing";
import type { TestApplicationBuilder, TestProviderOverride } from "@aponiajs/testing";
import type { TestApplicationOptions, TestServer } from "@aponiajs/testing";
```

- `createTestApplication(rootModule, options?)` — returns the builder. The root is anything the factory accepts: a decorated class, a `DynamicModule`, or a `ModuleDefinition`. `options` is `AponiaApplicationOptions`, with one difference: `logger` defaults to `false`.
- `TestApplication` — the boot. `application`, `get(token)`, `handle(request)`, `listen()`, `close()`, and `Symbol.asyncDispose`.
- `TestApplicationBuilder` — `overrideProvider(token)` and `compile()`.
- `TestProviderOverride` — `useValue`, `useFactory`, `useClass`, `useExisting`.
- `TestServer` — `url` and `webSocketUrl`, the `http://` and `ws://` forms of the one bound socket.

## Booting and asserting without a server

```ts
import { createTestApplication } from "@aponiajs/testing";
import { AppModule } from "../src/app.module.ts";

const application = await createTestApplication(AppModule).compile();

try {
  const response = await application.handle(new Request("http://localhost/users"));
  expect(response.status).toBe(200);
} finally {
  await application.close();
}
```

`handle` binds no port, and a case that only calls it never opens a socket. `await using application = ...` is the shorter form: `TestApplication` is an `AsyncDisposable`, and `close()` is idempotent.

## Replacing a provider

```ts
const application = await createTestApplication(AppModule)
  .overrideProvider(UsersRepository)
  .useValue({ findById: async () => undefined })
  .compile();
```

An override is keyed by the token the graph provides, and the rewrite walks the whole compiled graph, so a provider an imported module exports is replaced wherever in the graph it lives. The application's own module is never touched, so two boots from one module class share nothing. `useFactory(factory, inject?)` and `useClass(Substitute, inject?)` state their dependency tokens explicitly, because a hand-written stub carries no decorator metadata. Declaring the same token twice is one decision, and the later declaration wins.

Nothing is compiled until `compile()` is called — an override rewrites the compiled graph, so it is declared before the boot rather than applied to a running application. With nothing overridden, `compile()` hands the root straight to `AponiaFactory.create` and the boot is that call exactly.

## A real socket

```ts
const server = await application.listen();
const socket = new WebSocket(`${server.webSocketUrl}/chat`);
```

Port `0` asks the operating system for a free port and `getUrl()` reports the one it granted, so nothing reserves a port and releases it first — the dance that leaves a window in which another process takes the port before the application binds it. Nothing else in this package opens a port.
